newsitem.title: USA: San Francisco board okays domestic partners rules.
newsitem.headline: San Francisco board okays domestic partners rules.

text.p: San Francisco's governing board approved legislation Monday that would bar the city from signing contracts with companies that do not offer the same benefits to domestic partners as married couples.
The San Francisco Board of Supervisors approved the proposal, which seeks to extend the benefits to gay and lesbian couples, by a vote 10-0, sending it to Mayor Willie Brown for his approval.
The legislation, believed to be the first of its kind in the nation, was an important victory for the city's politically powerful gay and lesbian community, the proposal's authors said.
Brown spokesman P.J. Johnston said the mayor was likely to sign the legislation.

"The mayor supports the concept of equal rights and benefits for domestic partners," Johnston said. "He won't sign until he's seen it. But in concept, the mayor's very supportive. It's the kind of legislation that the mayor is likely to sign."

The legislation, if enacted, would require companies wishing to do business with San Francisco to provide benefits to the domestic partners of their employees if they provide them to the spouses of their employees.
The legislation covers benefits such as bereavement leave, medical leave and health insurance. The legislation does not require companies to provide benefits that they do not already provide spouses.
If enacted, city officials said the new law would affect thousands of private companies seeking to do business with San Francisco.

"This bill is cutting-edge legislation," Supervisor Leslie Katz said in a recent statement. "It is the first time a major city has taken action to ensure domestic partner benefits are provided by the private sector."

The legislation was brought to the Board of Supervisors by the Harvey Milk Lesbian/Gay/Bisexual Democratic Club. "It is obviously a major priority to the gay community," said Supervisor Tom Ammiano, who introduced the proposal in May.
Ammiano said the local Catholic church had written a letter to the city asking the supervisors to put off Monday's vote.
